papers.title: The Reporting and Methodological Recommendations for Observational Studies Estimating the Effects of Deprescribing Medications (REMROSE-D) ISPE-Endorsed Guidance.
papers.one_line: Consensus guidance for observational studies of deprescribing, built from a systematic review of 45 studies and a modified Delphi, centering on defining the deprescribing exposure, defining time zero, and avoiding immortal time.
papers.what_was_done: Deprescribing, the supervised stopping, reducing or tapering of medications, is hard to study observationally and had no reporting standard. The guidance was built in two stages. Stage one drew candidate recommendations from a systematic review of 45 studies published between January 2000 and September 2023, from which 78 items on study characteristics and methods were extracted; candidates were selected where reporting was frequently missing, where studies varied widely, or where an item was judged critical to this design, an example being whether a minimum medication-free interval is specified to define that deprescribing occurred. Stage two ran a modified Delphi to reach consensus on inclusion, modification or exclusion. The systematic review had found variability in reporting and potential for major bias concentrated on two things: how deprescribing was measured as an exposure, and immortal time introduced by that exposure measurement. The resulting recommendations focus on reporting detailed deprescribing treatment strategies, defining time zero, avoiding immortal time, and addressing confounding by indication. The guidance is endorsed by the International Society for Pharmacoepidemiology.

future_research.gap: Before this guidance no established standard existed for designing or reporting these studies, and the review identified priority areas rather than resolving them.
future_research.quote: Pharmacoepidemiologic studies on deprescribing are challenging to implement, yet little guidance exists on methods to avoid bias and minimum reporting for replicability and appraisal.

problems.evidence: Deprescribing has no settled operational definition, and the review found the measurement of the exposure to be the single largest source of variability across 45 studies. The example the guidance gives of a critical item is whether a minimum medication-free interval is specified, which is the question of how long an absence of dispensing must run before it counts as stopping. The recommendation is to report the strategy in detail rather than to supply a rule for grouping the versions.
problems.quote: This systematic review identified variability in reporting and potential for major biases, primarily related to the measurement of deprescribing as an exposure and introducing immortal time related to exposure measurement.

problems.evidence: Time zero and immortal time appear in the guidance's own summary as two of its four focus areas, which means a Delphi panel identified them as the places these studies fail rather than as settled practice. The link the review found is structural: the immortal time is introduced by how the exposure is measured, so fixing the timing means fixing the exposure definition, and the guidance supplies reporting requirements for both rather than a selection procedure.
problems.quote: To adequately address potential biases, these recommendations focus on the reporting of detailed deprescribing treatment strategies, defining time zero, avoiding immortal time, and addressing confounding by indication.

problems.evidence: A consensus list of reporting items and methodological considerations now exists for one design, derived from measured deficiencies in a systematic review rather than from opinion alone, and endorsed by a professional society. It is a reporting checklist for deprescribing studies rather than an inventory separating what a study could interrogate from what it can only assume, and confounding by indication, its one identification item, is listed alongside items about definitions.
problems.quote: We developed consensus recommendations for the methods and reporting of observational studies that aim to examine the effects of deprescribing.

papers.title: Time-related Bias When Studying Perinatal Complications After Maternal Injuries: Application to Maternal Injuries and Preterm Birth.
papers.one_line: Shows that the apparent protective effect of third-trimester maternal injury on preterm birth reported across the literature is an artifact of treating injury as a time-fixed exposure, reversing an adjusted odds ratio of 0.73 into a hazard ratio of 1.22.
papers.what_was_done: Studies of maternal injury and preterm birth have reported inconsistent results, and the literature stratifying by trimester has repeatedly found lower or even protective risks for third-trimester injuries, across injury types from minor trauma to assaults. The structural reason is that an injury occurring after 37 weeks cannot precede a preterm birth, so classifying a pregnancy as exposed if injured at any point mixes exposures that were never at risk of the outcome. This retrospective cohort of 58,897 births in one health system from 2018 to 2024 identified maternal injuries in 1,801 women, 3.1 percent, and compared a time-fixed logistic analysis against a Cox analysis with a time-varying injury definition and follow-up restricted to periods when the pregnancy was at risk of preterm birth. The time-varying analysis gave an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.16 for any injury, with an interval of 1.01 to 1.32, and positive associations in all trimesters rising to 1.17 and 1.22 for the second and third. The time-fixed analysis gave 1.01 for any injury and a significant protective association for third-trimester injury, an adjusted odds ratio of 0.73 with an interval of 0.54 to 0.98. Restricting follow-up to seven days after injury raised the estimate further, to 1.82 with an interval of 1.03 to 3.20.

future_research.gap: Two alternative designs are named for the same problem, a sequential target trial emulation and a time-matched nested case-control, without any comparison of them.
future_research.quote:
For example, emulating a sequential target trial with observational data would help align the start of
follow-up with exposure timing and avoid immortal time
bias.27,28

problems.evidence: The reported trimester gradient in an entire literature is shown to be a timing artifact rather than biology: with follow-up restricted to the period when the pregnancy is actually at risk, third-trimester injury has the strongest positive association, and with the time-fixed definition it appears protective at conventional significance. Only one prior study in this area had treated injury as time-varying. The failure is invisible in the reported output, since the protective odds ratio looks like a substantive finding and has been interpreted as one.
problems.quote:
Our results suggest that this trend
is primarily driven by the immortal time bias, as time-fixed
analyses typically underestimate associations for 3rd trimester
injuries.

problems.evidence: How much follow-up counts as at risk after an injury is a protocol component with no observable answer, and the estimate moves with it: any injury during pregnancy gives 1.16, and restricting to the seven days after an injury gives 1.82. Both are reported, and they answer different questions about how long an injury's effect persists, which the data cannot settle.
problems.quote: In analyses restricting the follow-up to 7 days postinjury, results suggested higher risks of preterm birth following injury (e.g., adjusted HR for any injury 1.82 [1.03, 3.20]),

papers.title: Effect of immortal time bias on the association between immune-related adverse events and oncological outcomes following immune checkpoint inhibitors therapy for head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
papers.one_line: Re-estimates the association between immune-related adverse events and survival in head and neck cancer with a landmark analysis and an extended Cox model, halving the apparent benefit and removing it for progression-free survival.
papers.what_was_done: Immune-related adverse events have been proposed as markers of checkpoint inhibitor benefit, and a meta-analysis of 29 studies in solid cancers is reported to have included only seven that considered immortal time. This retrospective single-institution study of 130 patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma treated with checkpoint inhibitors compared naive analyses against a landmark analysis and an extended Cox model that carries the onset time as a time-dependent variable, with sensitivity analysis over landmark times. Odds ratios for response and disease control were smaller under the landmark analysis than under the naive one. For progression-free survival the adjusted hazard ratio for these events was 0.49 with an interval of 0.28 to 0.85 in the proportional hazards analysis and 0.75 with an interval of 0.40 to 1.40 in the extended Cox analysis; for overall survival it was 0.36 with an interval of 0.19 to 0.66 against 0.51 with an interval of 0.27 to 0.95. The conclusion is that these events remain an independent prognostic factor for overall survival but not for progression-free survival, and that the association is overestimated when immortal time is ignored. Events were ascertained retrospectively by chart review without prespecified criteria, defined as those requiring corticosteroids or hormone replacement, so mild self-resolving events were likely missed and onset timing was often hard to determine.

future_research.gap: Whether these events are usable as on-treatment markers remains open, and future work is asked to account rigorously for immortal time.
future_research.quote: Future research should explore more thoroughly the role of irAEs as potential on-treatment markers for ICI outcomes, ensuring that analyses rigorously account for immortal time bias to provide accurate and reliable conclusions.

problems.evidence: Correcting the timing changes one of the two conclusions: progression-free survival goes from a significant hazard ratio of 0.49 to a nonsignificant 0.75, and overall survival from 0.36 to 0.51. The prior literature is reported to be built largely on the uncorrected version, with seven of 29 studies in a meta-analysis handling it. The correction that reverses the finding is not visible in the reported estimate, only in the modeling choice.
problems.quote: Without considering the immortal time bias, the association between irAEs and oncologic outcomes in patients with HNSCC treated with ICIs was overestimated.

problems.evidence: The exposure is defined by a retrospective judgment about whether an adverse event was immune-related, made from charts with no prespecified criteria, operationalized as requiring corticosteroids or hormone replacement. Mild events that resolved on their own were therefore missed, and the paper states that the timing of onset is often hard to determine. In a design whose whole point is when the exposure occurred, the onset date is itself a measurement with unquantified error.
problems.quote: Furthermore, distinguishing whether these mild AEs are truly immune-related is often challenging, and accurately determining the timing of irAE onset can also be difficult.

problems.evidence: The two remedies applied to the same data disagree about progression-free survival, and the paper prefers the extended Cox model on the argument that landmark analysis excludes patients and loses power, citing a prior study in the same disease whose landmark analysis dropped a large number of patients and performed no time-dependent analysis. Which of the two a study reports determines whether it finds an association.
problems.quote: However, the study had a large number of patients excluded by landmark analysis, which reduced its statistical power.

papers.title: An Eternal Dilemma: Exposing the Impact of Immortal Time Bias on Antifibrotic Effectiveness.
papers.one_line: Editorial comparing two studies that both corrected for immortal time in the same clinical question and reached opposite primary results, tracing the divergence to inclusion criteria, index date, censoring and follow-up length rather than to the correction.
papers.what_was_done: No randomized trial has shown a mortality benefit for antifibrotics in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, while observational studies repeatedly have, and every one of those has been argued to carry immortal time bias. The editorial reviews a new study that treats antifibrotic therapy as a time-dependent variable, with subgroup analyses, multivariable adjustment and a simulation study, and finds no significant mortality benefit overall; ignoring the immortal time, whether by exclusion or misclassification, restores a significant difference. Subgroups tell a different story: a nonsignificant trend toward benefit among those starting within two months, and a significant benefit when that early-start group is restricted to those over 65. The editorial then compares this against an earlier Medicare study by an author of the editorial, which used a time-varying Cox model, also addressed immortal time, and found a significant mortality reduction. The differences it identifies are inclusion criteria, the index date definition, first diagnosis alone against first diagnosis or first fill, censoring rules, a gap of 45 days or more without a fill in the earlier study, and follow-up length. It singles out the censoring decisions as most likely to explain the divergence, and raises the exposure definition question directly.

future_research.gap: How much adherence should be required before a patient counts as exposed is unresolved, and adherence to these drugs varies widely in practice.
future_research.quote: If not, what is the appropriate degree of compliance to most accurately evaluate their effectiveness in real-world clinical practice?

problems.evidence: The editorial asks whether a single prescription, under thirty days of medication, should count as exposure to a sustained therapy, and answers that nobody knows what degree of compliance defines the strategy. It cites an antiplatelet study in which progressively stricter definitions of treatment continuation moved the results, with the strictest definition coming closest to the randomized trials. The versions of the treatment are therefore known to matter and are grouped by whatever rule the analyst adopts.
problems.quote: In the case of the antifibrotics, should a patient who only receives a single prescription for an antifibrotic (i.e., <30 d of medication) really be classified as exposed to therapy?

problems.evidence: Two studies of the same drugs and the same outcome, both handling immortal time with a time-varying exposure, reach opposite primary conclusions. The differences the editorial can point to are all design choices with no principled setting: who is eligible, whether the index date is first diagnosis or first fill, whether to censor at a gap in dispensing, and how long to follow. Correcting the bias both studies set out to correct did not make their results transferable to each other, let alone to a new question.
problems.quote: There are several key differences between the methodologies of these studies, such as their inclusion and exclusion criteria (the Mayo study only included those older than 65 yr, and their index date definition only included first diagnosis of IPF rather than first diagnosis or date of first fill in this study), censoring decisions (the Mayo study censored for a gap of ≥45 d without a prescription fill), and follow-up period (the prior study did not limit follow-up to 2 yr).

problems.evidence: The divergence between the two studies is attributed principally to censoring: one censored patients who stopped therapy, which the newer study argues introduces selection bias. Censoring at discontinuation is an artificial censoring that requires the reasons for stopping to be captured, and it was applied as a rule about dispensing gaps rather than as an identifying assumption with a stated adjustment.
problems.quote: Xu and colleagues raise a valid concern regarding the censoring of patients who stopped therapy in the Mayo study, which could have introduced selection bias.

papers.title: Characteristics of non-randomised studies of drug treatments: cross sectional study.
papers.one_line: Assesses 200 representative non-randomised drug studies against the three time points a target trial fixes, finding 70 percent carry at least one time-alignment bias, 2 percent report all six key elements, and 3 percent have an available protocol.
papers.what_was_done: A random sample of Medline-indexed reports of comparative non-randomised studies of drug effectiveness or safety, published in June to August 2022, was screened until 200 eligible reports were found; 262 of 462 identified were excluded, 32 percent for having no comparator and 25 percent for not accounting for confounding. Each was assessed against eligibility, treatment assignment and start of follow-up using a form built from RECORD, STROBE, CONSORT, the target trial framework, STaRT-RWE and ROBINS-I. Of the 200, 70 percent had at least one possible bias from misalignment: prevalent users included in 24 percent, post-treatment eligibility criteria in 32 percent, immortal time periods in 42 percent, and treatment classification problems in 23 percent. Only 11 percent had a comparator, accounted for confounding, and had no time-alignment bias or dealt with all of them. Reporting was incomplete: 2 percent reported all six key elements considered. Most studies, 67 percent, used routinely collected data, while 7 percent reported using validation studies of the codes or algorithms used to select the population, 7 percent mentioned registration on a trial registry, and 3 percent had an available protocol.

future_research.gap: Tools are needed that let researchers report study elements comprehensively and adopt the target trial framework, which the survey found almost nobody doing.
future_research.quote: The robustness and transparency of non-randomised studies should be improved by providing tools for researchers to take advantage of the availability of routinely collected data, comprehensively report study elements, and facilitate the adoption of the target trial emulation framework
future_research.locator: How this study might affect research, practice, or policy

problems.evidence: In a representative sample of the current literature, 42 percent contained immortal time and 32 percent applied eligibility criteria evaluated after treatment, so misalignment of the three times is the norm rather than the exception. Only 11 percent of studies cleared all three requirements, a comparator, adjustment for confounding, and no unresolved time-alignment bias. The framework that names these three times has existed for a decade and had reached almost none of this literature.
problems.quote: Of the 200 included reports, 70% had one possible bias, related to: inclusion of prevalent users in 24%, post-treatment eligibility criteria in 32%, immortal time periods in 42%, and classification of treatment in 23%.

problems.evidence: Three percent of these studies had an available protocol and seven percent mentioned a registry entry. There is therefore no record of what any of them intended before the analysis, let alone of the eligibility thresholds, comparators, washout windows and outcome definitions that were considered and rejected. The alternatives are not merely unrecorded; the final protocol is unrecorded too.
problems.quote: Most studies used routinely collected data (67%), but few reported using validation studies of the codes or algorithms applied to select the population (7%), mentioned registration on a trial registry (7%), or had an available protocol (3%)

problems.evidence: Two percent of studies reported all six elements the assessors considered key, which are the elements needed to tell whether the design is sound at all. Assessment of what a study assumed and what it could check is therefore impossible for the other 98 percent from the published report, and the survey had to judge design type from prespecified criteria rather than from what the authors called it.
problems.quote: Reporting was incomplete, and only 2% reported all six of the key elements considered: eligibility criter

problems.evidence: Two thirds of these studies define their population from codes or algorithms in routinely collected data, and seven percent report any validation of those algorithms. The exposure, outcome and eligibility variables therefore enter as error-free classifications in the great majority of the current literature, with no accompanying estimate of their accuracy.
problems.quote: few reported using validation studies of the codes or algorithms applied to select the population (7%)

papers.title: Emulating target trials of postexposure vaccines using observational data.
papers.one_line: Specifies several target trials for postexposure vaccination, emulates them through nested daily sequential trials starting from exposure date, and works out the eligibility, confounding and variance consequences for mpox.
papers.what_was_done: Postexposure vaccination is hard to trial because participants must be found, randomized and vaccinated inside the window between exposure and symptom onset, and its effectiveness varies sharply with time since exposure, which makes estimates from trials with different vaccination time distributions incomparable. The paper defines three causal questions about postexposure vaccines, each with its own estimand and hypothetical trial, and shows how each can be emulated from health care records or contact tracing data, with a full protocol for mpox and a step-by-step emulation. The incubation period and the distribution of vaccination times are placed at the center of both design and emulation. Eligibility in the emulation must match the trial, which rules out restrictions based on post-baseline events such as excluding those vaccinated late or after symptoms. To avoid immortal time, follow-up must start so that the distribution of time since exposure is the same in both arms, which is achieved by emulating nested daily sequential trials from the exposure date: each day, eligible participants are identified and assigned by whether they were vaccinated that day, with unvaccinated participants serving as controls in multiple trials until they are vaccinated or develop symptoms. Per-protocol effects are obtained by censoring at deviation and adjusting with a g-method. Simulations compare this against two naive strategies, and code is released.

future_research.gap: Emulating a trial of postexposure vaccination on transmission would need close follow-up or random testing of contacts and may be compromised by behavior change under a lack of blinding.
future_research.quote:
Emulating a trial of the effect of postexposure vaccination on transmission would
require close follow-up or even random testing of the contacts of
the vaccinated and unvaccinated participants, and the emulation
may be compromised by changes in exposure behaviors due to
lack of blinding in most observational settings.

future_research.gap: Eligibility depends on knowing who is actually at risk, which requires exposure classification, vaccination and infection history and symptom screening that routine data may not supply.
future_research.quote: More broadly, when emulating postexposure trials, determining eligibility requires knowing who is actually at risk of infection.

problems.evidence: The registry entry says sequential emulation creates repeated participation whose dependence the efficiency gain conceals. Here the dependence is stated as a consequence of the design rather than left implicit: an unvaccinated participant serves as a control in every daily trial until vaccination or symptoms, the observations are therefore not independent, and the standard errors must be adjusted by a cluster-robust variance estimator or the bootstrap. That covers the within-person dependence. Calendar-time confounding across the sequence, where the trials differ because the epidemic and the vaccination policy differ by day, is not addressed.
problems.quote: Additionally, because we are using the same participant in multiple nested trials, our observations are no longer independent. Therefore, appropriate adjustment to our SEs is necessary to account for possible correlation across observations.

problems.evidence: The paper states the rule directly: eligibility in the emulation cannot use post-baseline events, and gives the two restrictions this literature actually applies, excluding those vaccinated more than fifteen days after exposure and excluding those vaccinated after symptoms. Both look like reasonable cleaning and both condition on what happened after time zero. The rule is available and the practice it forbids is standard.
problems.quote: In particular, this means we cannot include restrictions based on post-baseline events (eg, “exclude those vaccinated more than 15 days after exposure or those vaccinated after symptoms”), because these may introduce bias and would be unavailable at baseline in the target trial.

problems.evidence: Two devices for residual confounding are written into the emulation protocol rather than left to a discussion section, with concrete instances for this question: negative-outcome controls chosen so that the confounding structure is shared but the outcome is plausibly unaffected by vaccination, such as routine visits standing in for health-seeking behavior or a positive syphilis test standing in for high-risk sexual behavior, and a sensitivity analysis over a plausible range of unmeasured confounding strength. What is missing is any rule connecting what a negative control shows to what the estimate should become.
problems.quote: One strategy is to identify possible negative-outcome controls,21,22 that is, outcomes where confounding structure is expected to be similar but are plausibly unaffected by vaccination.

problems.evidence: For this class of question the timing rule is derived rather than conventional: because effectiveness depends on time since exposure, the start of follow-up must be chosen so that the distribution of time since exposure matches across arms, and the daily nested design achieves that by construction from the exposure date. Simulations show what the naive alternatives cost. The rule depends on an observable exposure date and on knowing the incubation period distribution, so it does not extend to strategies whose grace period is a clinical choice rather than a biological interval.
problems.quote: To avoid immortal time bias, we need to choose a start of follow-up in the emulation in a way that ensures the distribution of time since exposure is the same in both groups.25

papers.title: Antifibrotics and mortality in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: external validity and avoidance of immortal time bias.
papers.one_line: Estimates the effect of antifibrotics on mortality in the Japanese national claims database by two immortal-time-controlling routes, a time-dependent Fine-Gray model and a target trial emulation, which give materially different hazard ratios and are reported as agreeing.
papers.what_was_done: Pooled randomized trial analyses suggested antifibrotics improve survival in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis on short-term data from strictly selected patients, and observational studies suggested the same without controlling immortal time. This study used the Japanese National Claims Database to estimate an intention-to-treat effect, covering 30,154 patients with the diagnosis of whom 14,525 received an antifibrotic between 2013 and 2018, and treating lung transplantation as a competing event. Two approaches were used, each with a new-user design: multivariable Fine-Gray models with antifibrotic initiation as a time-dependent covariate, and a target trial emulation. The time-dependent models gave adjusted hazard ratios of 0.85 for nintedanib, with an interval of 0.81 to 0.89, and 0.89 for pirfenidone, with an interval of 0.86 to 0.93. The emulation gave 0.69, with an interval of 0.65 to 0.74, and 0.81, with an interval of 0.78 to 0.85. The paper reports the emulation as replicating the associations. Subgroup analyses covered age, sex and comorbidity categories, with interactions found for renal and peripheral vascular disease and nintedanib. Diagnoses came from claims codes without confirmation by multidisciplinary discussion, and no pulmonary function measurements exist in the database, so long-term oxygen therapy was substituted as a severity adjustment.

future_research.gap: Whether one antifibrotic outperforms the other, and in which subgroups, is not addressed and would need the same data used differently.
future_research.quote: For example, determining whether pirfenidone or nintedanib demonstrates better efficacy in reducing mortality or identifying preferable antifibrotic agent based on subgroups could provide useful information for the selection of antifibrotic treatments.

problems.evidence: Two analyses of the same data, both designed to control immortal time and both using a new-user design, give hazard ratios of 0.85 and 0.69 for the same drug, a difference larger than either confidence interval spans. The paper reads the second as replicating the first and presents the agreement as evidence of robustness. Nothing in the reporting establishes which estimand each targets or why they differ, and a reader given either alone would have no way to know the other existed.
problems.quote: The TTE model also replicated the associations of nintedanib (aHR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.65–0.74) and pirfenidone (aHR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.78–0.85) with reduced mortality.

problems.evidence: The disease defining eligibility is an administrative code assigned by an attending physician, and the paper states it could not establish whether any diagnosis rested on the multidisciplinary discussion that defines this condition clinically. Specificity was pursued by excluding codes for causes of secondary interstitial disease, which is a rule rather than a validated algorithm, and the severity measure that would have been the main confounder, pulmonary function, is absent from the database entirely.
problems.quote: The IPF diagnoses were made by the attending physician at each hospital, but it could not be established whether these diagnoses were based on multidisciplinary discussion (MDD).

problems.evidence: Lung transplantation is handled as a competing event rather than as censoring, which is the right structure for an outcome that transplantation makes impossible and that treatment plausibly affects. The choice is stated in the methods with the estimator that implements it, a Fine-Gray model. It is one decision made explicitly rather than a convention, and the paper does not state which causal effect the resulting subdistribution contrast corresponds to.
problems.quote: To address immortal time bias, we employed models treating antifibrotic initiation as a time-dependent covariate and target trial emulation (TTE), both incorporating new-user designs for antifibrotics and treating lung transplantation as a competing event.

papers.title: Addressing immortal time bias in precision medicine: Practical guidance and methods development.
papers.one_line: Compares landmark analysis, time-distribution matching and time-dependent analysis for immortal time, proposes multiple imputation of the unknown index date instead, and applies it to a single-arm precision oncology program.
papers.what_was_done: Precision medicine is evaluated from single-arm programs against real-world comparators, where the immortal time is known for the intervention patients and unknown for the controls. The paper reviews the standard remedies and their failure modes: landmark analysis is the commonest in cancer evaluations but its results are highly sensitive to the landmark chosen, discards information from both arms, and imposes one landmark on everyone, which is inappropriate where genomic heterogeneity drives both access and response; time-distribution matching reduces information loss but assigns dates non-informatively, which can bias; time-dependent analysis performs well but needs delayed entry and time-varying confounding handled. It then treats the unknown immortal time as missing data and imputes it, giving step-by-step guidance on selecting the imputation method, specifying the imputation model, and pooling. The case study evaluates overall survival under whole-genome and transcriptome analysis against usual care for advanced cancers in British Columbia from 2012 to 2015, applying both time-distribution matching and imputation, with bootstrap simulation across missingness rates and sample sizes. Survival results did not differ substantively between the two, but standard errors were higher under imputation for every point estimate, and mean imputed immortal time was stable across simulations.

future_research.gap: The relative performance of the proposed imputation against cloning and against the prevalent new-user design has not been established, and would need a simulation study.
future_research.quote: Establishing the relative performance of these competing approaches versus MI is an important avenue for further investigation.

future_research.gap: Sensitivity analysis over the choice of landmark time is recommended and uncommon, and how the frequency and performance of landmark analysis vary in this field is uncharacterized.
future_research.quote: The frequency and performance of landmark analysis in precision medicine evaluations is not systematically characterized.

problems.evidence: The paper reframes the timing problem as one of missing data: the length of the immortal period is known for the intervention arm and unknown for comparators, so it can be imputed conditional on patient characteristics rather than fixed by a landmark applied uniformly. The gain is that uncertainty about the true length enters the standard errors rather than being assumed away, and the method does not need a landmark chosen by the analyst. It rests on missingness at random and on ignorability, neither testable, and the estimates in the case study matched the simpler alternative.
problems.quote: Compared to alternative approaches, MI minimizes information loss and better characterizes statistical uncertainty about the true length of the immortal time period, avoiding false precision.

problems.evidence: Four remedies for one problem are laid out with distinct failure modes, none dominating: landmark analysis is sensitive to a parameter the analyst picks and discards data, time-distribution matching assigns dates that carry no information, time-dependent analysis needs further assumptions about delayed entry and time-varying confounding, and imputation needs missingness at random. The paper states that the relative performance of these against each other has not been established, so a study picking one has no evidence to cite.
problems.quote: Landmark analysis is straightforward to apply and by far the most common approach in cancer‐related evaluations, but results and conclusions are sensitive to the choice of landmark time and information loss across both intervention and control patients can drive estimation bias.

problems.evidence: The proposed method converts a design problem into a missing data problem, which means the estimate now rests on an assumption about the missingness mechanism. The paper states plainly that the immortal time is unlikely to be missing completely at random, adopts missing at random plus ignorability instead, and notes that ignorability cannot be tested because the mechanism is unobserved. The recommended response is a sensitivity analysis under alternative missingness models.
problems.quote: The ignorability assumption cannot be tested given that missing data and their underlying mechanism are unobserved, but sensitivity analysis assuming different missing data models, including missing not at random (MNAR), can be examined to characterize stability of results.

papers.title: Designing target trials using electronic health records: A case study of second-line disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs and cardiovascular disease outcomes in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.
papers.one_line: Demonstrates target trial emulation in electronic health records for adding a second-line antirheumatic drug to methotrexate, and describes the design process as iterative, with protocol components revisited in light of artifacts found in the data.
papers.what_was_done: Whether adding a biologic or targeted synthetic antirheumatic drug to methotrexate reduces cardiovascular risk in rheumatoid arthritis is unsettled, with meta-analyses of trials finding no reduction and a meta-analysis including observational studies finding benefit, a discrepancy attributed to selection bias, immortal time bias and unmeasured confounding. The study emulates an open-label pragmatic trial in electronic health records from a regional academic health system, contrasting methotrexate alone against methotrexate plus a second-line drug, with major adverse cardiovascular events as the outcome. The stated purpose is instructional: to supplement existing guides with design and implementation detail for a question where treatment can be initiated at many time points, which the paper offers as a more principled alternative to comparing never against ever initiators. It notes that only 200 emulations were published between March 2012 and October 2022, a quarter using electronic health records, of which 30 were cardiological. The design process is described as iterative, with components specified first and revisited according to what the data turn out to contain, and collaboration with clinicians called essential so that analytic decisions do not create implausible clinical situations. No difference in risk was observed, consistent with the trial meta-analyses.

future_research.gap: The framework has barely reached cardiovascular research, with 30 emulations classified as cardiology across a decade.
future_research.quote: This TT approach has not been widely adopted in cardiovascular health research.

problems.evidence: The paper states as recommended practice what the registry entry describes as the mechanism of the problem: the protocol is drafted, the data are examined, and the components are revised in light of what the data contain. The revision is justified by clinical plausibility rather than by anything that separates data features from outcome-relevant information, and the analysis that follows conditions on the revised protocol as if it had been fixed in advance. Only 3 percent of studies in this literature publish a protocol, so the revisions leave no record.
problems.quote: The design process is iterative: key components are described at the beginning and may need to be revisited based on artifacts in the observational data source.

problems.evidence: The emulation is read against previously published trial meta-analyses of the same question, and the agreement is offered as support for the interpretation rather than as validation of the method. That is closer to what the entry asks for than a binary replication verdict, since it treats the trial evidence as a reference point for a result rather than as a pass mark. It is a single comparison against a pooled estimate, with no accounting of how closely the estimands, populations or measurements align.
problems.quote: Benchmarking results of observational analyses to previously published RCTs can lend credibility to interpretation.

papers.title: Causal Inference Challenges in the Relationship Between Social Determinants and Cardiovascular Outcomes.
papers.one_line: Reviews what causal inference requires of social determinants of cardiovascular health, showing that well-defined exposure and consistency fail for constructs proxied by education and income, and that some determinants cannot be expressed as manipulable treatments at all.
papers.what_was_done: The review examines definitions and measures for social determinants of cardiovascular health, then works through what multivariable analysis of observational data requires for a causal reading: well-defined exposure and the consistency assumption it supports, then confounding, selection bias, information bias and positivity. Well-defined exposure is identified as the hardest requirement here, because social determinants are seldom simple atomistic interventions that can be conceptualized and measured. Information bias is treated at length: correcting measurement error requires a gold standard, and social exposures have none, with education and income standing in as very crude proxies for broader social processes and years of attained education being a poor measure even of education. The conclusion distinguishes determinants such as race and political ideology, which are close to impossible to express as manipulable treatments, from education and income, which respond to interventions and can in principle be studied as treatments. It recommends discrete policy changes over an individual's social status measured once, natural experiments such as job loss or lottery wins, self-controlled designs comparing one person at two times, and target trial formulations, with attention to time-dependent confounding when exposure changes over time.

future_research.gap: Which underlying construct a simple social indicator proxies, and how far it sits from any theoretical gold standard, cannot be settled by consensus, so information bias in these measures cannot be addressed.
future_research.quote: it is difﬁcult to achieve consensus about what underlying constructs are being proxied by simple social indicators, and how one can begin to address information bias in relation to the distance between indicator and theoretical gold standard.66
future_research.locator: Additional Causal Inference and Statistical Considerations

problems.evidence: The review separates determinants that admit an intervention from those that do not, and places race and political ideology in the second group. For those, the protocol component that a target trial requires, a treatment strategy someone could be assigned to, does not exist, so the design cannot be specified rather than being difficult to emulate. For education and income it grants that policy changes give a manipulable version, which is a route rather than a procedure.
problems.quote:
Many social determinants, such as race and political
ideology, are almost impossible to express as manipulable
treatments.90

problems.evidence: Consistency requires that the exposure pick out a set of versions with a common effect, and the review states that social determinants are seldom the kind of simple atomistic intervention that can be conceptualized and measured that way. Its recommended fix is to study a discrete policy change instead of an individual's measured status, which replaces the exposure rather than partitioning its versions.
problems.quote:
Well-deﬁned
exposure is especially challenging for social determinants of health
because they are seldom simple atomistic interventions that are easily
conceptualized and measured.

problems.evidence: Correcting measurement error presupposes a gold standard against which the error can be assessed, and the review points out that for the constructs at issue none exists. Education and income enter analyses as crude proxies for broad social processes, and years of attained education is not even a good measure of education, so the distance between the recorded variable and the intended construct is unmeasurable rather than merely unmeasured.
problems.quote: This is nowhere more true than in the study of social determinants of health, in which very crude proxies, such as education and income, are meant to stand in for broader social processes.
problems.locator: Additional Causal Inference and Statistical Considerations

papers.title: Comparing broad and narrow phenotype algorithms: differences in performance characteristics and immortal time incurred.
papers.one_line: Quantifies, across 11 chronic conditions and five databases, the sensitivity and predictive value gained by requiring a confirmatory diagnosis code and the immortal time that requirement necessarily creates.
papers.what_was_done: Phenotype algorithms trade sensitivity against specificity, and a common device for raising specificity is to require a second diagnosis code. This study built five algorithms for each of 11 chronic conditions across five United States databases: one broad algorithm requiring a single code, and four narrow ones requiring a second code within 1 to 30, 1 to 90, 1 to 365, or any number of days of continuous observation. Performance was estimated with PheValuator, which uses predictive modeling rather than chart review and returns sensitivity and specificity as well as predictive value. Requiring a second code always raised positive predictive value and lowered sensitivity, with the 1 to 365 day window giving the highest predictive value and the 1 to 30 day window the lowest sensitivity. Immortal time was then computed as the interval from the index date to the earliest of the outcome, the end of the time at risk, or the second code, across four windows of time at risk from 30 to 1,095 days. The immortal time grew as the window for the second code widened, and its share of time at risk was highest for the shortest time at risk. The conclusion is that raising specificity this way is valid at the cost of incurring immortal time, and that caution is needed where the outcome is death or strongly associated with it. Reproducible algorithm definitions are published as JSON files.

future_research.gap: Alternatives to a confirmatory code that would raise specificity without buying immortal time, such as requiring a procedure or treatment shortly after the diagnosis, are suggested and not evaluated.
future_research.quote: Researchers with study designs where a narrow phenotype algorithm is needed might consider alternative approaches to using a second code, such as requiring a specific procedure or other treatment within a very short period following the diagnosis code.

future_research.gap: How much bias a given phenotype produces depends on several interacting quantities and has to be worked out case by case through quantitative bias analysis.
future_research.quote: including the distribution of TAR in the analysis, the background risk of mortality in the target population, the association of the outcome with mortality, and the shape of the hazard function over follow-up

problems.evidence: The registry entry says phenotypes enter emulations as error-free binary variables. Here the error is measured rather than assumed away: sensitivity and positive predictive value are estimated for five definitions of each of 11 conditions in five databases, using a method that returns specificity as well, which chart-review validations usually do not. The algorithms are released as reproducible definitions. What is not supplied is propagation: the performance figures are offered as inputs to a quantitative bias analysis the reader must perform, and exposure, outcome and eligibility misclassification are not carried jointly through any estimate.
problems.quote: We found that requiring a second code at any time after the index event (i.e., the occurrence of a condition code for the first time in a subject’s history) always increased the positive predictive value and decreased the sensitivity compared to single-code algorithms.

problems.evidence: The confirmatory-code requirement is a measurement decision that fixes a time interval, and the interval is immortal by construction: nobody can have the second code after dying. The study shows the immortal time grows with the confirmation window and that its share of time at risk is largest for short follow-up, which is where a short-horizon emulation lives. No procedure sets the confirmation window, and it is chosen for its effect on predictive value.
problems.quote: We also found that requiring a second code invariably adds immortal time to the subjects in these cohorts.

new_problems.proposed_title: Raising phenotype specificity buys immortal time, and nothing trades the two against each other
new_problems.statement: A confirmatory-code requirement is the standard device for raising the specificity of a phenotype, and the interval it waits for is immortal by construction, since the confirming code cannot appear after the outcome that ends follow-up. Specificity and immortal time therefore move together as a function of one parameter, the confirmation window, and no procedure sets that parameter by reference to the estimand. The two failures are also assessed by different people at different stages: the phenotype is validated once, often in a different database and for a different study, while the immortal time it creates is a property of the design that adopts it.
new_problems.why_open: Measured across 11 chronic conditions and five databases, widening the confirmation window monotonically raises positive predictive value and monotonically raises the immortal time incurred, with the immortal share of time at risk largest under short follow-up. A study can therefore reduce misclassification and increase time-related bias with a single choice, and report only the first. The available response is a study-specific quantitative bias analysis whose result depends on the time-at-risk distribution, the background mortality, the association of the outcome with mortality, and the shape of the hazard, so it cannot be precomputed with the phenotype. Alternatives that would decouple the two, such as requiring a procedure within a very short window, are suggested and unevaluated.
new_problems.quote: Attempting to increase the specificity of a health condition algorithm by adding a second code is a potentially valid approach to increase specificity, albeit at the cost of incurring immortal time.
new_problems.checked_against_index: MER-01 says phenotypes enter as error-free binary variables and asks for joint propagation of misclassification, which is about the error, not about a design bias the error correction creates. TZO-01 says no outcome-blind procedure selects the time grid or grace period, which covers intervals the analyst chooses as part of the strategy, not an interval inherited from a validated phenotype definition written for another purpose. DTA-03 concerns whether the same variable means the same thing across sources. None of the three states that specificity and immortal time are coupled through one parameter, which is what makes this actionable: it identifies a trade nobody currently makes explicitly.

papers.title: Association of Immune-Related Adverse Events and the Efficacy of Anti-PD-(L)1 Monotherapy in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: Adjusting for Immortal-Time Bias.
papers.one_line: Finds immune-related adverse events associated with better survival after adjusting for immortal time, with landmark times selected to maximize events in one direction and minimize losses in the other.
papers.what_was_done: Whether immune-related adverse events predict benefit from checkpoint inhibitors is contested, and the paper attributes the disagreement partly to how immortal time is handled. It retrospectively enrolled 425 patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer on anti-PD-(L)1 monotherapy between January 2016 and June 2021, 127 with such events and 298 without, with median follow-up 38.8 months. Landmark analyses at 2, 3, 6 and 9 months and a time-dependent Cox analysis were both applied. The association survived both: progression-free survival of 11.2 against 3.4 months and overall survival of 31.4 against 14.0 months. Organ-specific analyses found skin, thyroid and hepatic events associated with better survival while pneumonitis was not, and single-organ involvement outperformed multi-organ, which the paper attributes to higher rates of grade 3 or worse events and treatment discontinuation in the multi-organ group. Severe events and discontinuation were harmful, systemic steroids made little difference, and resumption trended favorable. The methodological discussion states why the literature disagrees: landmark analysis excludes early progression and late-onset events, cutting sample size and power, and results depend strongly on the landmark chosen, with published landmarks ranging from four weeks to twelve months.

future_research.gap: Both remedies applied may introduce new biases, which the paper states it can only try to minimize.
future_research.quote: Second, even though two methods, with their own advantages, were applied to eliminate the ITB, they may also create new biases.

future_research.gap: Why different organ-specific events carry different prognostic weight is unexplained, with severity and discontinuation offered as one candidate and immunopathogenic mechanism as another.
future_research.quote: However, why different organ-specific irAEs are related to different outcomes remains unsolved.

problems.evidence: The landmark times were selected by a criterion defined on the analysis data: maximize the number of patients who had developed the exposure by the landmark while minimizing the number who progressed or died before it. Both quantities are functions of the outcome, so the parameter that determines who enters the analysis was tuned against the data it analyzes. Published landmarks for this question span four weeks to twelve months, which is the range within which that tuning operates.
problems.quote: We set the landmarks at 2, 3, 6, and 9 months, aiming to maximize the number of patients developing irAEs while minimizing the number of patients having progression/death prior to the landmarks.

problems.evidence: The paper attributes the contradictory literature on this question to the choice of remedy rather than to the biology: studies using a time-dependent model mostly find an association and studies using landmark analysis mostly do not, and it argues the time-dependent model is better because it retains all events and follow-up. That makes the reported conclusion a function of a methodological choice that no study is required to justify or to report alternatives for.
problems.quote: Regardless of the statistical methods, we observed that the occurrence of irAEs was significantly associated with improved outcomes, similar to most studies using the time-dependent Cox model [ 10 , 14 , 18 , 20 ] but contrary to some studies using landmark analysis [ 12 , 14 ]. Such heterogeneous results might be explained by the limitations of the methodology.
